# Scott Galloway Voice Corpus

Research date: 2026-09-09 (spoken-register enrichment: 2026-10-18)

The excerpts below are short quotations from public No Mercy / No Malice newsletter posts and a public podcast transcript, included under fair use for style analysis and attribution. They are third-party content and NOT covered by this repository's MIT license.

**Provenance note.** Items 1-31 were read directly from profgalloway.com on the research date and are verbatim. Items 32-35 come from an ASR (auto-generated) YouTube caption track of a Prof G Pod episode, so wording may be imperfect; they are labeled `documented`, not verbatim.

**Punctuation note.** Nearly every excerpt below preserves an em dash because it is a verbatim quotation and dashes are a core, heavy feature of his written register. The operator's copy rule still bans em and en dashes in anything YOU generate in this voice; see the Punctuation Override in SKILL.md for exactly how to convert them.

   Same post. The self-deprecating cold open, told as a scene.

## Structural notes for the writer

- Section headers are never neutral. "Pwned," "Bubbleicious," "Real Problems," "Leverage." Each one alone tells you the verdict of that section.
- Every number is specific and usually has a named source attached inline (RAND, Bloomberg, the DEA, UC Berkeley researchers). A round, unsourced number is off-voice.
- Profanity shows up roughly once or twice per long post, always for one sharp beat, never scattered throughout.
- The self-deprecating personal anecdote almost always opens the piece, before any policy argument begins.
- Em dashes cluster: some paragraphs carry three or four. See the Punctuation Override in SKILL.md for exact counts per sampled post.

**Spoken register (added 2026-10-18 from items 101+):**
- Every spoken answer opens "Okay, so just some data." then a four-to-eight-item stat cascade with sources named inline, then "So let's take a step back" or "Here's the thing" into the argument, then "Anyways, appreciate the question." The written cold-open anecdote moves to the middle of the answer aloud.
- The rant is a numbered list that breaks: "One, demonstrate excellence. Two, accountability…" and the profanity or joke erupts inside item two or three, then the list resumes. Profanity runs higher aloud (roughly one "fuck" per answer, plus "shit", "bullshit", "asshole") and always for a single beat.
- Self-indictment before policy: the mistake first (sold everything in 2016, lost 40% of liquid net worth; "B-minus manager"), often with an aside about the cost of saying it ("by the way, I've lost a lot of viewers here"), then the generalization.
- Spoken pet phrases: "In sum", "See above [noun]", "Boss", "Get this", "By the way", "Anyways", "Here's the thing", "reductive analysis", "thinly veiled transfer of wealth from the poor to the rich and from the young to the old", "absence of anxiety", "winners and losers", "owners and earners", "word salad" (naming his own ramble), "that's real cabbage".
- Jokes are compressed inversions ("Academia is the only industry where they take away titles and prefixes as a promotion"; "99% of our children are not in the top 1%") plus pop culture as verdict (thunderdome, hunger games).
- Spoken vs written: longer sentences with mid-course corrections, stats delivered approximately ("I think it was Paul Tudor Jones who said"), pivots are vocal ("But here's the thing") rather than dash-shaped. Treat spoken numbers as approximate; the renamed-maxim move and the dead-empire analogy survive intact. No Mercy / No Malice audio is read by George Hahn, not Galloway.
